Dear all, 

I was trying the code in Section 5.5 of the manual with a set of data set (data set at the bottom of this post). 

stan.model3 <- '
data{
 int<lower=1> N;
 int<lower=1> K;   //num of categories
 int<lower=1> D;   //num of predictors
 vector[D] x[N];
 int y[N];
}
parameters{
 matrix[K, D] b;
}
model{
 for( k in 1:K){
 for( d in 1:D)
 b[k, d] ~ normal(0, 5);
 }
 for( n in 1:N )
 y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(b*x[n]));
}
'

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about multinomial logistic regression (results quite different from multinom() in R)
parts:
It looks like there are two differences.

First, it looks like the other package automatically added
an intercept. You need to do that explicitly in Stan
by either adding intercept parameters or adding a
column of 1 values in the data matrix. The former is more
efficient in most cases.

Second, it looks like the other package you're using
took the approach of using (D-1) coefficient vectors.
This is a standard strategy to identify a model for
maximum (penalized) likelihood estimation.

As a tip, I'd use categorical_logit rather than applying
a softmax transform --- it'll be more efficient and more
arithmetically stable.

Putting this all together, you can code the alternative approach up in Stan
as follows:

data {
int<lower=2> K; // num categories
int<lower=1> D; // num predictors (without intercept)
int<lower=0> N; // num observations
vector[D] x[N]; // predictors
int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N]; // observations
}
transformed data {
vector[1] zero;
zero[1] <- 0;
}
parameters {
vector[K-1] alpha; // intercepts
matrix[K-1,D] beta; // slopes
}
model {
// temps
vector[K] lambda;
lambda[1] <- 0;

// priors
alpha ~ normal(0,20);
// likelihood
for (n in 1:N) {
for (k in 2:K)
lambda[k] <- alpha[k-1] + beta[k-1] * x[n];
y[n] ~ categorical_logit(lambda);
}
}

Here's the fit with default params:

alpha[1] -1.95 0.02 0.74 -3.56 -2.43 -1.88 -1.44 -0.66 1153 1
alpha[2] -0.34 0.01 0.31 -0.92 -0.55 -0.34 -0.13 0.27 1625 1
beta[1,1] -39.67 0.26 9.52 -60.83 -45.53 -38.83 -32.94 -23.63 1312 1
beta[1,2] -12.99 0.22 7.30 -27.60 -17.79 -12.84 -7.92 0.60 1148 1
beta[2,1] -7.82 0.09 3.66 -15.66 -10.08 -7.63 -5.35 -1.11 1518 1
beta[2,2] 1.25 0.09 3.52 -5.48 -1.09 1.11 3.52 8.31 1420 1

Even with 1K+ effective samples, there's still substantial
std error in the posterior mean due to the very high posterior sd, which
itself is due to the small amount of data. So the priors may also
be having some effect, because they're informative for the model at hand
with its coefficients with abs values of 40.

But it's still pretty close to what the other program gave you,
so I trust the code:

You could always run Stan's optimizer to find a max (penalized)
likelihood solution, which may line up more closely with the other
program (you didn't say what kind of inference it uses and I'm not
an R expert nor do I have time to dig into it).

I've been meaning to add a discussion of the K vs. (K-1)
encodings of multinomial logit to the manual --- I just added
it to the longer-term to-do list.

- Bob

parts:
> On Feb 15, 2015, at 2:05 AM, Xiao He <xiao...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you, Bob. I have a couple of follow up questions.
>
> First of all, in your code, you have a section for transformed data. Is that section needed. I ask because zero is not is not used anywhere in the model section.
>
> transformed data {
> vector[1] zero;
> zero[1] <- 0;
> }
>
Sorry, that was just cruft left over from an earlier version.

In what sense? It's a different model for reasons outlined in my last mail
(no intercept, K coefficient vectors instead of (K-1)).

It's just the Bayesian posterior for the model you defined.

The main issue is identifiability because with K coefficient vectors, if you
add a constant to each one, you get the same answer. Of course, without an
intercept, you don't have a plain old additive term.

We were wrestling about which formulation to use, K versus (K-1), but
they both have their strengths and weaknesses. The nice part about (K-1)
is that it's identified even if there's an intercept. The nice part about
K is that it's symmetric in the categories, so the prior applies to all of them.

- Bob
